To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

exposure to volatile organic compounds (VOC) can cause liver disease, even in the absence of underlying liver disease, and that VOC-induced liver disease may be exacerbated when combined with underlying liver disease, such as non-alcoholic fatty-liver disease (NAFLD).
the interaction of volatile organic compounds (VOC) with underlying liver disease is a novel paradigm for risk.
volatile organic compounds (VOCs) induce oxidative stress in hepatocytes, which leads to the activation of multiple cell signaling pathways and ultimately to liver injury.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the identification of key molecular targets and pathways that are activated by exposure to industrial volatile organic compounds, as well as the identification of the molecular targets and pathways activated by the interaction of these toxicants with the underlying metabolic syndrome and/or liver disease.

the interaction of volatile organic compounds with the liver and how underlying liver disease may affect this interaction, with the aim of developing new strategies to better predict risk and prevent liver injury.
the interaction between volatile organic compounds and the liver, and how this interaction can be used to predict risk and to develop new therapeutic strategies.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the liver is an organ with a unique ability to adapt to environmental insults, and this ability is compromised by the presence of underlying liver disease, such as NAFLD.
the liver is a highly susceptible target organ, which can be injured by a variety of volatile organic compounds, and that this injury may be exacerbated by underlying liver disease.

volatile organic compound-induced hepatotoxicity is multifactorial and is mediated through a complex interplay of multiple signaling pathways, including oxidative stress, inflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction, lipid accumulation, endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress, and autophagy.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the liver is a complex organ with multiple functions and is vulnerable to toxicant-induced injury.
volatile organic compounds are capable of causing liver injury and that the underlying mechanism of this injury is dependent on both the chemical and the underlying disease state.
the combination of volatile organic compounds (VOC) and underlying liver diseases (ULDs) may be more dangerous than the VOC alone, as VOCs can exacerbate liver damage and disease.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the liver is a highly dynamic and complex organ that responds to environmental toxicants in multiple ways and that these responses may be synergistic and additive, depending on the underlying liver health of the individual.
the liver is an important organ for metabolism of volatile organic compounds, and that underlying liver disease, such as NAFLD, can be an important modifier of toxicant-induced injury.

the combination of toxicants with underlying disease, such as non-alcoholic fatty disease, can synergistically cause liver injury, and that the interaction of toxicants and underlying disease may be more important than exposure alone.
